prompt: A team estimates that untangling its billing module would take about four weeks. Meanwhile, each billing feature takes roughly two extra days because of the tangle, and billing changes several times a month. A product manager asks which figure is the **interest** on this debt. Which answer is right?

options.text: The four weeks, because that is what the debt will eventually cost
options.explanation: The four weeks is the principal: the one-off work to bring the code to the design you now want. Paying it stops future interest; it is not the interest itself.

options.text: The two extra days on each billing change, paid again every time someone works in the module
options.explanation: Correct. Interest is the recurring extra effort the current shape imposes. Cunningham: 'Every minute spent on not-quite-right code counts as interest on that debt.' Because it is charged per change, how often billing changes decides how fast the bill grows.

options.text: Neither; only deliberate shortcuts carry interest
options.explanation: How the debt arose (deliberate or inadvertent) is what Fowler's quadrant classifies. Inadvertent debt slows changes just as much, so it carries interest too.

options.text: The module's age: the interest grows with every month the tangle exists
options.explanation: This is where the financial metaphor breaks down. Fowler notes that code charges interest when someone works on it, not as time passes. An ugly module nobody changes costs little change effort.

workedExample:
1. Principal: the one-off work to fix the design, here about four weeks.
2. Interest: the extra effort each change pays because the fix has not been made, here about two days per billing feature.
3. Interest is charged per change, not per month, so a frequently changed module runs up interest quickly and a rarely touched one barely at all.
4. That is the comparison that justifies (or not) paying the principal: how much interest you expect to keep paying versus what the fix costs. Both numbers are estimates.

prompt: A team that designed carefully using its best available knowledge while building a new product says: "We've learned a lot from six months in production. Now we can see the domain model we should have built." Which quadrant of Fowler's model is this debt?

options.explanation: Reckless-deliberate is 'we don't have time for design': knowingly cutting corners. Nothing here suggests they skipped design.
That is 'what's layering?': a team unaware of good practice. This team designed carefully; they simply learned more.
Correct. This is Fowler’s “now we know how we should have done it” quadrant. A team can design carefully and still discover a better domain model through production experience.
Prudent-deliberate is a conscious trade-off made up front ('We must ship now and deal with consequences'). This debt was discovered after the fact.

workedExample:
1. Deliberate or inadvertent? They did not choose a shortcut; they discovered a better model later. **Inadvertent.**
2. Prudent or reckless? They built carefully with what they knew. **Prudent.**
3. Fowler identifies prudent-inadvertent debt as the kind Cunningham described: code that reflected the team's understanding at the time, which it now refactors to reflect what it has learned.

prompt: Which of the following are forms of technical debt? Select all that apply.

options.text: A web framework three major release versions behind, no longer receiving security patches
options.explanation: Correct. Dependency debt: deferred maintenance can accumulate migration work, and losing security support adds risk. Version numbers alone do not establish upgrade difficulty.

options.text: A payments service only one engineer understands, with no documentation
options.explanation: Correct. Knowledge debt (a bus factor of one). Every change and incident there waits on one person.

options.text: An integration test suite that fails randomly about 1 run in 10
options.explanation: Correct. Test debt: flaky tests slow every merge and train people to ignore failures.

options.text: A feature the product team decided not to build this year
options.explanation: That is a product decision about scope, not a property of the code. Nothing in the codebase is costing extra effort.

workedExample:
Use the definition: does it make future engineering work slower or riskier than it needs to be?

1. Unsupported framework: yes, losing security patches creates risk and deferred migration can add work.
2. One-person service: yes, knowledge is a bottleneck.
3. Flaky tests: yes, every pipeline run pays.
4. Unbuilt feature: no; it is a backlog item, not a cost on existing work.

prompt: A company has 120 microservices pinned to a logging library at version 2.x. Version 2 reaches end of security support in six months and version 4 is current. Each service team has always said upgrades "aren't a priority". What is the best explanation of why this is now expensive, and the best general prevention for the future?

options.text: Deferred dependency maintenance and rollout across 120 services are now concentrated before a support deadline; prevent recurrence with continuous upgrade assessment, automated update PRs and representative tests
options.explanation: Correct. Repeated deferral can accumulate migration and coordination work while reducing scheduling freedom. Small, regular upgrades can spread that work and expose incompatibilities earlier, but each release still needs review and testing.

options.text: Logging libraries are inherently hard to upgrade; prevention is to write your own
options.explanation: An in-house library moves the maintenance cost onto you rather than removing it, and still needs upgrading across 120 services.

options.text: The cost comes from having too many microservices; prevention is to merge them into a monolith
options.explanation: Service count multiplies the effort, but a monolith would also have fallen two major release versions behind. The root cause is deferring upgrades.

options.text: There is no real cost; teams can keep using version 2 indefinitely
options.explanation: Unsupported software may continue running, but newly discovered vulnerabilities may receive no vendor fix. Keeping it indefinitely can create unacceptable security and operational risk.

workedExample:
1. Inspect actual release notes and migration guides: a major version change may introduce incompatibilities, but the numbers alone do not prove which ones occurred.
2. Assess both migration steps and coordinate rollout across 120 services before security support ends.
3. Use automated update PRs, representative tests, release-note review and staged rollout so upgrades become routine. A green suite is evidence, not proof of safety.
4. Choose a support policy appropriate to the dependencies and service; merely staying one major version behind does not guarantee support. Continuous attention reduces accumulated work without guaranteeing cheap or risk-free upgrades.
